science.title: Global mismatches between drought trends and ecosystem resistance reveal emerging ecosystem vulnerability
science.description: Ecosystem resistance to drought is widely used to assess vulnerability under climate change, but its decline does not always coincide with worsening drought conditions. In this study, we evaluated the spatial correspondence between long-term changes in ecosystem resistance and drought trends across drought-affected areas of global terrestrial ecosystems, excluding irrigated lands. Using satellite-derived NDVI and SPEI at a spatial resolution of 5 arc-minutes, we evaluated Mann–Kendall trend Z scores for ecosystem resistance and four drought characteristics, namely drought duration, frequency, severity, and intensity, during 2002–2019, and classified their sign combinations into four categories. As a result, declining resistance was observed not only in regions where drought characteristics intensified, but also in regions where drought characteristics weakened. Moreover, even where drought-characteristic trends were non-positive, ecosystem resistance did not consistently show a positive trend. The distribution of the four categories also differed among land-cover types. In addition, comparison of height above nearest drainage suggested that categories associated with declining resistance tended to occur in relatively lower topographic positions. These results suggest that ecosystem resistance cannot be explained by meteorological drying alone, but instead reflects multiple vulnerability types shaped by hydrological conditions and ecosystem-specific sensitivity.

science.title: Scientists reveal why walking gets so much harder with age
science.description: As we age, the body appears to sacrifice walking efficiency in exchange for stability. Older adults stiffen the ankle more with each step, which may help prevent falls but also forces the muscles to work harder while producing less forward motion. This leads to shorter strides, slower walking, and faster fatigue. Exercises targeting balance, coordination, and lower-leg strength could help preserve mobility.

science.title: Examining the impact of nano-titanium dioxide on the adhesion and failure behavior of asphalt mixtures in acid rain conditions
science.description: This study investigates the combined effects of nano-TiO₂ modification and environmental pH conditions on the performance of asphalt mixtures, with a particular focus on moisture susceptibility, fatigue resistance, low-temperature cracking, and surface free energy (SFE) characteristics. Nano-TiO₂ was incorporated into the asphalt binder at a fixed dosage of 5% by weight of binder, selected based on previous optimization studies reported in the literature. The results indicate that nano-TiO₂ modification significantly improves the overall performance of asphalt mixtures. Specifically, fatigue life increased by approximately 45% under dry conditions compared to the control mixture. However, under acidic exposure (pH 4), both modified and unmodified mixtures exhibited a reduction in fatigue performance, although the nano-TiO₂ modified mixtures consistently showed higher fatigue resistance than the control samples across all environmental conditions. Similarly, improvements in moisture resistance and fracture performance were observed in modified mixtures, although the magnitude of improvement was influenced by environmental pH. SFE analysis further revealed that nano-TiO₂ enhances both cohesive and adhesive energy components of the binder, while acidic conditions reduce surface polarity and weaken interfacial interactions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that nano-TiO₂ modification improves the intrinsic durability of asphalt mixtures; however, environmental acidity plays a critical role in governing the extent of performance improvement. These results highlight the importance of considering environmental exposure conditions when evaluating the long-term behavior of nanomodified asphalt systems.
